titel: Gross, net and the marginal tax rate
kurz: How income tax and social security contributions, two deduction systems with opposite logic, lead from gross to net pay, and why the marginal tax rate is decisive for almost every financial decision.

bloecke.md: Between the salary in your employment contract and the amount that arrives in your account lie two deduction systems that follow opposite rules. Income tax is progressive and open-ended at the top. The higher the taxable income, the larger the share that goes in tax. Social security contributions, by contrast, are levied at a fixed percentage, but only up to a ceiling. No contributions are due on income above it. With only one of the two rules in mind, you regularly reach wrong conclusions, for example that working more no longer pays above a certain salary, or that top earners always hand over the largest percentage.

## Structure of the income tax schedule

The income tax schedule is laid down in Section 32a EStG (Income Tax Act) as a calculation rule, not as a table. The tax base is taxable income (zu versteuerndes Einkommen, zvE), that is, income after deducting income-related expenses (Werbungskosten), special expenses (Sonderausgaben) and allowances. Gross pay is not the relevant measure.

In 2026, no tax is due on taxable income up to €12,348. This basic tax-free allowance (Grundfreibetrag) is meant to keep the subsistence minimum free of tax. The first euro above it is taxed at 14%. After that, the rate rises *continuously* rather than in steps. In the first progression zone, up to €17,799, it climbs steeply from 14% to 23.97%; in the second, it rises more gently to 42% at €69,878. From €69,879 it stays constant at 42%, and from €277,826 at 45%.

The steepest rise in the schedule is therefore in the lower income range. This shape is known as the middle-class bulge (Mittelstandsbauch). The 42% rate begins at a taxable income of just under 1.3 times the median earnings of a full-time job, which stood at €54,066 gross a year in 2025. A single person with statutory insurance and no children who deducts only the lump-sum allowances in addition to their pension and insurance expenses (Vorsorgeaufwendungen) reaches this taxable income at around €87,000 gross, that is, at 1.6 times median earnings. The so-called top tax rate (Spitzensteuersatz) therefore already affects skilled workers and salaried employees. The rich tax rate (Reichensteuersatz) of 45% only applies at a taxable income of just over five times these earnings. With joint assessment, the schedule is applied to half of the couple's combined taxable income and the result is doubled. In effect, this doubles all the thresholds.

bloecke.md:
## Marginal tax rate and average tax rate

The [[marginal tax rate]] shows how much tax is due on the next euro earned. The [[average tax rate]] shows what share of total income already goes in tax. Both figures relate to the same income and differ considerably.

At a taxable income of €50,000, income tax under the 2026 schedule is around €10,548. The average tax rate is therefore 21.1% and the marginal tax rate 35.1%. This difference follows from the basic idea of progression. The high rate applies only to the top slice of income and never to the whole income. Because the marginal tax rate never rises above 45%, there is no point in the German schedule at which more gross pay leads to less net pay. Of every additional euro, at least 55 cents always remain before surcharges and social security contributions.

bloecke.unter: The gap between the two curves shows why a pay rise is never taxed away completely. Own calculation from the schedule formula in Section 32a EStG, separate assessment, excluding solidarity surcharge and church tax.

bloecke.md: The average tax rate is useful for looking back, for example to assess last year's tax burden. For every decision about overtime, a side job, a donation, a retirement contribution or further training, only the marginal tax rate counts, because each of these decisions changes only the top slice of income.

## Solidarity surcharge and church tax

The solidarity surcharge and church tax are surtaxes (Zuschlagsteuern). They are calculated on the assessed income tax, not directly on income. The solidarity surcharge (Solidaritätszuschlag, Soli for short) remains unchanged at 5.5%. However, it only applies once the assessed tax exceeds an exemption threshold (Freigrenze) of €20,350 (€40,700 with joint assessment). Even then, a phase-in zone (Milderungszone) applies first, in which it rises gradually to the full rate. As a result, the great majority no longer pay any solidarity surcharge on their employment income. This does not apply to capital income. There, the solidarity surcharge is levied directly on the flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer), without an exemption threshold.

Church tax is 8% of income tax in Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg and 9% in the other federal states. It is deductible without limit as a special expense, so the net burden is below the nominal rate. As a rough estimate, church tax at 9% raises the marginal burden in the proportional zone by around two percentage points; without the special expense deduction it would be just under four.

## Social security contributions as the second deduction system

Social security contributions are not taxes, because they are matched by an individual entitlement to benefits. In the net pay calculation, they nevertheless work like a tax. They differ from income tax in three respects. There is no basic allowance, the contribution rate is proportional rather than progressive, and the obligation to contribute ends at a ceiling.

bloecke.titel: Social security rates and contribution assessment ceilings (Beitragsbemessungsgrenzen) 2026

bloecke.md:
The additional contribution (Zusatzbeitrag) in the table is an average across the health insurance funds. Your own fund may be below or above it. Switching funds is one of the rare cases in which the same benefits can be had for less. Childless people aged 23 and over pay a supplement of 0.6 percentage points in long-term care insurance, which they bear alone. Their employee share therefore adds up to around 21.75%. From the second child onwards, the contribution rate falls in stages.

Above the [[Contribution assessment ceiling (Beitragsbemessungsgrenze)|contribution assessment ceiling]], no further contributions are due. This has a consequence that is missing from most debates about progression. The *marginal burden*, meaning tax and contributions combined on the next euro, does not rise continuously with income. It rises up to the ceilings and drops at each of them: for the single person in the illustrative calculation below, by around 7 percentage points at the ceiling for health and long-term care insurance and by around 6 percentage points at the ceiling for pension and unemployment insurance. The drop is smaller than the contribution rates that fall away, because the contributions reduce taxable income as deductible pension and insurance expenses. Beyond that, the marginal burden grows only with the tax schedule.

The calculation assumes a single person aged 30, with no children and no church membership, in statutory health insurance with the average additional contribution and no other income.

1. Social security contributions are 21.75% of €60,000, that is, €13,050 (pension 5,580, health 5,250, long-term care 1,440 including the supplement for the childless, unemployment 780). Neither ceiling has been reached yet.
2. Taxable income is around €46,700. It is calculated as €60,000 minus the employee lump-sum allowance (Arbeitnehmer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,230 minus deductible pension and insurance expenses of around €12,100 (retirement provision plus basic health and long-term care insurance).
3. Income tax under Section 32a is around €9,400. The average tax rate on taxable income is 20.1%, the marginal tax rate 34.0%.
4. No solidarity surcharge is due, because €9,400 is below the exemption threshold of €20,350.
5. Net pay is €37,550, around €3,130 a month. Total deductions amount to 37.4% of gross pay.

The marginal burden, which this list does not show, is more revealing. Of €1,000 more gross pay, around €510 remains here; €218 goes to the social security funds and around €271 to the tax office.

bloecke.md:
## The marginal tax rate and financial decisions

Every euro that reduces taxable income saves tax at the marginal tax rate, not at the average tax rate. This applies to income-related expenses above the lump-sum allowance of €1,230, to special expenses, to extraordinary expenses and to salary sacrifice (Entgeltumwandlung) into an occupational pension. A donation of €1,000 costs €580 net at a marginal tax rate of 42%, but €750 at a marginal tax rate of 25%. For the same donation to the same recipient, the net cost therefore differs by €170; at a marginal tax rate of 25%, it is just under 30% more expensive.

Three conclusions follow from this. First, subsidised retirement provision that reduces taxable income today and is taxed as income later pays off precisely when the marginal tax rate in retirement turns out lower than today. You should check this assumption rather than simply take it for granted. Second, a flat-rate tax is only favourable as long as your personal marginal tax rate is above it. The 25% on capital income is an advantage for high earners. For low earners it is a disadvantage, which they can recover through their tax return. Third, timing matters. If a year with high income and one with low income lie ahead, it pays to shift deductible expenses into the high-income year, because the same receipt saves more tax there.

Tax classes (Steuerklassen) do not change the amount of annual tax. They only determine how much wage tax is withheld during the year. The final annual tax depends solely on annual income and is settled through the assessment. The III/V combination brings liquidity forward and often leads to additional tax payments; the IV/IV combination with a factor distributes the deduction more accurately. The tax class does play a role where wage replacement benefits are based on net pay. Before parental leave, the choice of tax class therefore has financial consequences.

The [[progression proviso (Progressionsvorbehalt)]] makes tax-free benefits more expensive. Parental allowance (Elterngeld), short-time work allowance (Kurzarbeitergeld), unemployment benefit (Arbeitslosengeld) and sickness benefit (Krankengeld) remain tax-free themselves, but raise the tax rate on the rest of your income (Section 32b EStG). Anyone who has received such benefits is required to file a tax return, and additional tax is often due.

- Work out your own marginal tax rate once and remember it. With it, almost every decision that costs or saves money can be converted into net amounts.
- Foreseeably high income-related expenses or extraordinary expenses can be registered with the tax office in advance as an allowance (wage tax reduction procedure, Lohnsteuer-Ermäßigungsverfahren). Net pay then rises immediately, not only after the assessment.
- Compare your health insurance fund's additional contribution with the average once a year. At €60,000 gross, a difference of half a percentage point amounts to around €150 a year in employee share, for unchanged benefits.
- Calculate in marginal net amounts, but negotiate in gross. On every gross euro, the employer pays around 20% on top as the employer's share.

bloecke.titel: Schedule formula for checking the figures
bloecke.md:
For taxable income between €17,800 and €69,878, the following applies in 2026:

`z = (taxable income - 17,799) / 10,000`

`Income tax = (173.10 × z + 2,397) × z + 1,034.87`

For a taxable income of €50,000, z = 3.2201. So income tax = (173.10 × 3.2201 + 2,397) × 3.2201 + 1,034.87 = 2,954.40 × 3.2201 + 1,034.87 = €10,548.

The marginal tax rate is the derivative of this formula, that is, `(2 × 173.10 × z + 2,397) / 10,000`, here 35.12%. The constant of €1,034.87 corresponds to the tax at the upper end of the previous zone. That is why the schedule has no jump.

mitnehmen: Income tax is progressive and has no upper limit; social security contributions are proportional and capped by a ceiling.
The average tax rate describes the burden in retrospect; for every new decision, the marginal tax rate is what counts.
Because the marginal tax rate stops at 45%, there is no step in the German schedule at which more gross pay leads to less net pay.
Because of the contribution assessment ceilings, the marginal burden does not rise continuously; at €120,000 gross, more of the next euro remains than at €60,000.
Tax classes only shift the deduction during the year; the final settlement is always based on annual income.

begriffe.text: Tax rate on the next additional euro earned. It is decisive for every decision about additional income or deductible expenses and lies between 14% and 45% in 2026.
Total income tax divided by taxable income. It is always lower than the marginal tax rate and only meaningful in retrospect.

Tax base of the income tax schedule. It is the income that remains after deducting income-related expenses, special expenses, extraordinary expenses and allowances, and it is not the same as gross pay.
Income ceiling up to which social security contributions are levied. In 2026 it is €5,812.50 a month for health and long-term care insurance and €8,450 for pension and unemployment insurance.
Rule in Section 32b EStG under which tax-free wage replacement benefits such as parental allowance or short-time work allowance raise the tax rate applied to the rest of your income.
